title: Buddy Petit comes to Covington; Rene joins his band and appears in the photo
summary: Rene recalls Petit's band arriving by train, being hired as pianist for the summer, posing in the field photo, and later seeing it in Esquire.

bands.name: Joe Liggins and His Honey Drippers

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends

blocks.x: Well, I don't know. First time that Buddy Petit came to Covington, I remember that very well. Because it probably was a Saturday night dance he had to play for. And so he did, he had to play this for, it was a white dance that was down in the Pavilion, that I recall, down by the river, Bofilaya River. And he got off the train and seated this customer at that time, naturally, for the band to play something at the station. You know, and we, so that everybody in town could know. It's just like broadcasting that I'm in town, that the dance will be held so the people could come. And so he blew some tunes down there that was out of this world. I'll never forget it because I heard it several blocks off, about maybe six or seven, eight blocks. You could, you know, it traveled, you know, those trumpets playing at night like that in the country town. So I ran down the station, that Buddy Petit was playing, you know, New Orleans jazz. Nothing in the country, that was just the greatest thing in the world, something to come into town like that, especially to give a dance. Now, I want to find out where the dance is, and probably everybody in town would be around the hall. That's what probably happened. And so we all actually listened a while, and when the band went to play at that particular dance, and then never mind, people would stand around, around the outside, a distance from the band, and listen to the music all night long. And he was a great, great band. And of course, later on, he was going to stay there for a while and play that territory for the summer. And of course, they told him that I was a piano player. And he said, come on down to Southern Hotel, and I'll see what you can play, what you know. So I went down to Southern Hotel, and he had a dance he was playing on there, and I played a few bars on the piano with him, the blues he was playing, which was easy. And he liked the way I was playing. He said, boy, you play all right. He said, I think I can use you. He said, I'll give you $3 a night. I think it was $3 a night or $3 a week. I'm not sure. But whatever it was, I never did get it. I think he gave me half of the amount. And I worked all summer, and I was so glad to work with his band. I didn't care whether they paid me or not. So that was kind of introduction to Buddy P.T. And that picture you see in the field. We played in Mandeville. And of course, there was nobody in the hall, and they said, they're going to take a picture of the band. Boy, come on out here. And I said, well, I can't. I play the piano. He said, well, you can't bring the piano. Pick something up and put it in your hand. Take that megaphone there and bring it on out there. So I had a cap on. I took the cap, put it on. I had my cap and I put it down. My eyes went out in that hot sun out in the middle of the field. And they took the picture. And I didn't realize when I took that picture that that picture would come back to be, not to haunt me so much, as to be a classic in the jazz field. Because Buddy P.T. was one of the greats. Yeah. And he, when I saw that picture in Hollywood, when I made success in my record company, exclusive records had arrived. And we had Joe Liggins and his Honey Drippers, the number one all over the country, right during the Louis Jordan area. And we were making money like mad with the $1.05 record. And I was getting my suits made at Cy DeVoza all across the street and sailing pretty high. And so I said, look at this. I see, I saw your picture in the Esquire. Well, I thought maybe it was going to find pictures, going to show me Esquire. And show me this Buddy P.T. picture of the old jazz guys. And he said, that's you with that funny hat on your head, cap on your head. I said, no, that's not me. He said, well, that looks like you. It surely looks like you. I thought it was going to disgrace me. You know, I said, this guy, wait a minute. I was thinking. And so I said, ah, sure, that's you. So I looked and I looked and I looked and I said, well, that might be me. I remember praying with Buddy. He said, sure, that's you. I said, I think that is me. And that's when I saw that picture for the first time. And it was in Esquire, all year, all jazz greats. I think Louis Armstrong's picture was in there. Buddy, all of us pictures on the first page.
